items.title: The simple type-A Hecke modules are indexed by e-regular partitions
items.statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, let
$e=e(F,q)\in\{2,3,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ be the quantum characteristic
([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]) and let
$H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for $n\ge0$. For $\lambda\vdash n$ let $S^{\lambda}$ be the
Hecke Specht module and $D^{\lambda}=S^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}$ its
cell-form quotient ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]). Then:

1. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if $\lambda$ is $e$-regular
   ([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]);
2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\vdash n\text{ is }e\text{-regular}\}$ is a complete
   set of pairwise non-isomorphic absolutely irreducible $H$-modules;
3. $H$ is split semisimple if and only if $e>n$ (including $e=\infty$); when
   $e\le n$ the algebra has nonzero radical.

This is the exact root-of-unity replacement for the ordinary Specht
classification. At $q=1$ in characteristic $p>0$ it specialises to the
classification of the simple $F[S_n]$-modules by $p$-regular partitions
([[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]). No
semisimplicity is assumed and no choice principle is used.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Use finite joint-primary projections without presupposing which labels survive. The regular right module has a cellular filtration with quotients copies of the cells; refining their common flags in [F3] gives a simultaneous triangular flag on it. Thus each $L_a$ is annihilated by a polynomial $\prod_b(X-b)^N$, with finitely many diagonal values $b\in F$ and $N\ge\dim H$. Polynomial Bezout and the Chinese remainder construction give $p_{a,b}$ congruent to one modulo $(X-b)^N$ and zero modulo the other factors. Substituting $L_a$ gives commuting idempotents. For a joint word $\xi$, their product $P_\xi$ is idempotent in $H$ and on a cell flag has diagonal one exactly at tableaux with word $\xi$, zero elsewhere. An idempotent has zero image if and only if all these diagonal entries vanish: its triangular matrix would otherwise be nilpotent and idempotent, hence zero. The vector-space functor $M\mapsto MP_\xi$ is exact on $H$-modules, because a lift $x$ of $y=yP_\xi$ can be replaced by $xP_\xi$, and kernels are preserved. No centrality or $H$-submodule assertion for this image is needed. [F3, F5, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 For finite $e$, equality of two diagonal values $[a]_q,[b]_q$ is equivalent to $a\equiv b\pmod e$. Indeed $[a]_q-[b]_q=q^b[a-b]_q$ for all integers, including negative integers. When $q\ne1$, $e$ is the multiplicative order of $q$, and when $q=1$, $e=\operatorname{char}F$ and the q-integer is the integer reduced to $F$. Thus a joint word is exactly a residue word in the node convention $c-r\pmod e$. [given, F3, F6, algebra]

1.3 Prove the complete ladder-boundary comparison. Put $L(s,c)=(e-1)s+c-e$. Suppose $\alpha$ is restricted, every occupied node has $L<l$, and the addable ladder-$l$ set is nonempty. Set $C=l+e-1$, $T=\lfloor C/(e-1)\rfloor$, $d=C-(e-1)T\in\{0,\ldots,e-2\}$ and $u_s=C-(e-1)s$. For $1\le s\le T$, $0\le\alpha_s\le u_s$, and no positive row occurs beyond $T$. The deficits $h_s=u_s-\alpha_s$ are nonnegative and satisfy $h_{s+1}-h_s=\alpha_s-\alpha_{s+1}-(e-1)\le0$. An addable ladder-$l$ row has deficit zero; thereafter every deficit is zero. Consecutive such rows have width difference $e-1>0$, so the ladder addables form a terminal interval $s_0,\ldots,T$. A first equality row that is not addable simply precedes this interval. Adding its bottommost $k$ nodes therefore adds in rows $T-k+1,\ldots,T$. The length of $\alpha$ is $T$ for $d>0$ and $T-1$ for $d=0$, including the empty case $T=1,d=0$. If $\beta\unrhd\alpha$ has the same size, its length is at most that of $\alpha$, by the prefix inequality at that length. For $d=0$ all addable rows of $\beta$ are at most $T$. For $d>0$ the sole possible extra row is $T+1$, with residue $-T$, different from $i=l\bmod e=d+1-T\bmod e$ since $1\le d+1<e$. Hence every addable $i$-node of $\beta$ lies in a row at most $T$. If $\gamma$ adds any $k$ of these initial addables, at row cutoff $r$ its prefix increment is at least $\max(0,k-\max(T-r,0))$, exactly the increment for the bottommost-$k$ extension $\delta$ of $\alpha$. Adding $\beta$'s prefix inequalities proves $\gamma\unrhd\delta$. This holds for every $k$ simultaneously and needs no same-content premise. [given, construct, algebra]

1.4 The integral intersection factorization. Work over $A=\mathbb Z[Q,Q^{-1}]$. Suppose a row-standard tableau $t$ already agrees with $t^\eta$ on rows before $j$, and let $B$ be the canonical label interval of row $j$. In rows $r\ge j$ let $\beta_r$ count its $B$-labels. First rearrange labels inside $B$ into increasing row-reading order, then do the same with all remaining tail labels, preserving the number of labels from each interval in every row. This gives a tableau $v$ whose row $r$ consists of a $B$-segment of length $\beta_r$ followed by a tail-segment of length $\eta_r-\beta_r$. The sorting removes inversions separately within the two label intervals, so $d(t)=d(v)wa$ with additive length, $w\in S_B$, and $a$ a permutation of the remaining tail labels. The intervals are disjoint, so $T_a$ commutes with $x_B$, and $T_wx_B=Q^{\ell(w)}x_B$. Let $K'$ be the subgroup cutting each canonical row $r\ge j$ into lengths $\beta_r,\eta_r-\beta_r$, while retaining the earlier rows. Let $K$ cut $B$ into consecutive lengths $\beta_r$ and the tail into consecutive lengths $\eta_r-\beta_r$, again retaining earlier rows. The permutation $d(v)$ increases on these segments on both sides and transports $K'$ to $K$. Hence $x_{K'}T_{d(v)}=T_{d(v)}x_K$, by expansion into length-additive standard-basis words. If $E$ consists of the minimal representatives with $S_\eta=\bigsqcup_{u\in E}uK'$, then $x_\eta=\sum_{u\in E}T_ux_{K'}$. Write $\nu=(\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_{j-1},\eta_j,\eta_j-\beta_j,\ldots,\eta_k-\beta_k)$, omitting zero parts. Multiplication of $x_K$ by $x_B$ gives $[\beta]!_Qx_\nu$: the $B$-intersection subgroup contributes $\sum Q^{\ell(b)}=[\beta]!_Q$, while its tail and earlier-row factors commute with $x_B$. Consequently the exact identity is $x_\eta T_{d(t)}x_B=Q^{\ell(w)}[\beta]!_Q\sum_{u\in E}T_uT_{d(v)}x_\nu T_a$. No scalar is divided out. Sorting $\nu$ to a partition uses the invertible block-reordering identity in [F5], so this is in $[\beta]!_Q Hx_{\nu^+}H$. If $\nu^+\ntrianglelefteq\eta$, the dominance-ideal assertion in [F5] makes its shape-$\eta$ part vanish. Otherwise the first $j+1$ largest parts of $\nu$ have sum at least $\eta_1+\cdots+\eta_j+\eta_j-\beta_j$; comparison with $\eta$ gives $\beta_j\ge\eta_j-\eta_{j+1}$. [F5, construct, algebra]

2.1 Canonical-row support without factorial cancellation. The semistandard permutation-basis theorem [[lem-type-a-hecke-permutation-modules-have-semistandard-murphy-bases-and-specht-filtrations]], followed by star, gives an exact coordinate condition for $Hx_\rho$: every supported right Murphy tableau has semistandard type $\rho$. Apply it to the factor remaining after $[\beta]!_Q$ in step 1.4, before putting back $T_a$. This factor belongs to $Hx_\nu$. In shape $\eta$, semistandardness forces the first $\eta_1$ labels into the first row, the next $\eta_2$ into the second, and so on through $B$: a label cannot occur below its own row, and each earlier row is already full. Thus its right tableaux have the first $j$ canonical rows. The permutation $a$ uses only later labels. Expanding $T_a$ by the row action and straightening cannot alter these canonical rows: their prefix counts are maximal, and same-shape straightening increases every tableau-prefix count by that supplier's Statement. This proves the canonical-row assertion even for the quotient by the displayed factorial. Starting at $j=1$, repeat steps 1.4 and 2.1 for each surviving standard-tableau term. If $\eta_j-\eta_{j+1}\ge e$, every surviving term at that stage has $\beta_j\ge e$, so $[e]!_Q$ divides its factor $[\beta]!_Q$. Later multiplication and integral straightening preserve this common divisor. This establishes the full repeated-symmetrizer support and divisibility used below. [F5, step 1.4, algebra]

2.2 For restricted $\eta$, number its nodes by increasing $L$, taking lower rows first on a tie, to obtain $t_\eta$. Moving right increases $L$ by one and moving down by $e-1$, so it is standard. The diagrams $\alpha_l$ of nodes with $L<l$ and $\delta_l$ with $L\le l$ are restricted: their row widths are the minimum of the restricted widths of $\eta$ and the positive part of the affine cutoff bound, each having adjacent difference at most $e-1$. A node on ladder $l$ forces every lower positive position on that ladder to be occupied, since $\eta_{s+1}\ge\eta_s-(e-1)$. Thus $\delta_l$ adds the bottommost $a_l$ ladder addables to $\alpha_l$. Any competing standard tableau with the same full residue word has, in the corresponding block, $a_l$ additions all of residue $l$. Every such node was addable before the block: adding an $i$-node creates new addable corners only of residues $i+1,i-1$, distinct from $i$ for $e\ge2$. Starting with the empty diagrams, step 1.3 inductively shows its shape dominates $\delta_l$ at every completed block, and hence its final shape dominates $\eta$. No strictly lower shape has the word of $t_\eta$, and no same-shape tableau uniqueness is asserted. [step 1.3, construct, algebra]

3.1 Choose $P_\xi$ for the word of $t_\eta$. It has nonzero image on $C_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$ and zero image on every $C_{\mathrm M}(\rho)$ with $\rho\lhd\eta$, by steps 1.2 and 2.2. Therefore it has zero image on their form quotients. Apply the exact projection to a composition series of $C_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$. Some constituent has nonzero image; by [F1] and [F4] it is a nonzero $D_{\mathrm M}(\rho)$ with $\rho\unlhd\eta$. The exclusion forces $\rho=\eta$, proving the restricted Murphy quotient nonzero over the original field. This is a joint-word and cellular-support proof, not an import of cellular/crystal label identification. [F1, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 If $\eta_j-\eta_{j+1}\ge e$ for some $j$, every surviving term at that row has $\beta_j\ge e$ by steps 1.4 and 2.1 and is divisible by $[e]!_Q$. Later multiplication and straightening cannot remove this polynomial factor. Every Gram entry is the coefficient of $x_\eta$ in $x_\eta T_{d(s)}T_{d(t)}^*x_\eta$ modulo higher shapes; first expand its middle factor in the row-module basis and apply the proved row calculation. Thus every entry is divisible by $[e]!_Q$. Specializing $Q$ to $q$ makes that factor zero, so the entire Murphy form vanishes and $D_{\mathrm M}(\eta)=0$. This concerns a common divisor of entries, not a product-of-hooks formula for a determinant. Combining with step 3.1 proves the finite-$e$ Murphy criterion. [F1, F5, step 1.4, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 For $e>n$, including infinity, distinct standard tableaux of any shapes have distinct full diagonal words. At their first unequal step the preceding diagram has size $a-1$; its distinct addable-corner contents differ by a nonzero integer of absolute value at most $a\le n$, so their q-integers differ. Induction recovers every next node. Consequently every tableau word of $C_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$ occurs in no strictly lower cell. Exact projections as in step 3.1 and diagonal multiplicity one in [F4] show that all $\dim C_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$ flag factors occur in $D_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$; thus this quotient has the full cell dimension and its form radical is zero. In particular at $e=\infty$ every partition is restricted and has nonzero quotient. At $n=0$ the unique cell is $F$ with norm one. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Establish the complete semisimplicity clause. Put $f_\eta=\dim C_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$ and $d_\eta=\dim D_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$, with zero for a zero quotient. The Murphy basis gives $\dim H=\sum_\eta f_\eta^2$. On each nonzero quotient its nondegenerate form and the cell law supply all rank-one operators. Since the cells are right modules, their action gives a surjective algebra map $H\to\operatorname{End}_F(D_{\mathrm M}(\eta))^{\mathrm{op}}$, a full matrix algebra after transpose. Its kernels are distinct maximal two-sided ideals: equality would give the same matrix-algebra simple module, contradicting [F1]. They are pairwise comaximal. Their finite product map is surjective: for each kernel $I_a$ and each other $I_b$ choose $u_{ab}\in I_b$ congruent to one modulo $I_a$, multiply over $b\ne a$, and use these elements to isolate each prescribed matrix component. Its kernel is the radical by the complete simple list and [F6]. Hence $\dim(H/\operatorname{rad}H)=\sum_\eta d_\eta^2$. Step 4.2 makes this equal to $\dim H$ when $e>n$, giving an isomorphism with a product of full matrix algebras over $F$. When finite $e\le n$, the one-dimensional Murphy row cell has norm $[n]!_q=0$, since $x_{(n)}^2=[n]!_q x_{(n)}$. Its quotient dimension is zero while its cell dimension is one; every other $d_\eta\le f_\eta$. The dimension sum is therefore strictly smaller and $\operatorname{rad}H\ne0$. This proves both directions of part 3 without any claim that some Specht module must be reducible. [F1, F5, F6, step 4.2, algebra]

6.1 Apply the same exact involution to every Murphy quotient: $D^\lambda=D_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ is nonzero exactly when $\lambda'$ is restricted, equivalently when $\lambda$ is regular. The nonzero quotients remain pairwise distinct absolutely simple and complete by [F1] and [F2]. This proves parts 1 and 2, and step 5.1 gives part 3. At $q=1$, [F6] gives precisely the ordinary $p$-regular group classification, including characteristic two; no splitting or semisimplicity assumption was made. All selections and polynomial computations were finite, so no choice principle is used. [F1, F2, F6, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 5.1] ∎

items.title: The type-A Hecke decomposition matrix is dominance unitriangular
items.statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, $e=e(F,q)$ and $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$
([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]). For
$\lambda\vdash n$ and $e$-regular $\mu\vdash n$ let
$$d_{\lambda\mu}:=[S^{\lambda}:D^{\mu}],$$
the multiplicity of $D^{\mu}$ in a composition series of the Specht module
$S^{\lambda}$ ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]],
[[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]]). Then
$$d_{\mu\mu}=1\qquad\text{and}\qquad d_{\lambda\mu}\ne0\ \Longrightarrow\ \mu\unrhd\lambda,$$
where $\unrhd$ is the dominance order on partitions
([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]): a simple factor $D^{\mu}$ of
$S^{\lambda}$ can occur only if the $e$-regular label $\mu$ dominates
$\lambda$. Equivalently the decomposition matrix $(d_{\lambda\mu})$ is
unitriangular along dominance. This constrains but does not compute the
entries: no off-diagonal decomposition number is determined by cellularity.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Invariance of composition multiplicities under the normalisation: by [F1] the twist $(-)^\theta$ is an exact equivalence of module categories with inverse $(-)^\theta$ itself, so it is additive on short exact sequences and carries composition series to composition series; hence $[S^{\lambda}:D^{\mu}]=[S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}]$ for all $\lambda\vdash n$ and $e$-regular $\mu\vdash n$. [given, F1, F4]

2.1 Vanishing: if $d_{\lambda\mu}\ne0$, then $[S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}]\ne0$ by step 1.1, so $\lambda'\unrhd\mu'$ by [F2], and conjugation reversal [F3] gives $\mu\unrhd\lambda$. [step 1.1, F2, F3]

2.2 Diagonal: taking $\lambda=\mu$ in step 1.1 gives $d_{\mu\mu}=[S^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}]=1$ by [F2]. [step 1.1, F2]

3.1 Assembly: steps 2.1 and 2.2 are exactly the two claims; ordering the rows and columns of $(d_{\lambda\mu})$ by any linear extension of dominance displays the unitriangular shape, and no off-diagonal entry is determined by the cellular structure. At $q=1$, [F1] and [F4] identify the same ordinary group labels; over a splitting p-modular system this agrees with [[thm-symmetric-group-decomposition-matrix-is-dominance-unitriangular]] within that supplier's hypotheses. The present proof establishes the bound over every field. [F1, F4, step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

items.title: Jantzen layer dimensions sum to the Gram determinant valuation
items.statement:
In the setting of [[def-jantzen-filtration-of-a-lifted-cell-module]] ($R$ a PID,
$\pi$ a prime element, $F=R/\pi R$, $M$ free of finite rank with a form whose
extension to $K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ is non-degenerate), let $\nu_\pi$ be
the $\pi$-adic valuation normalised by $\nu_\pi(\pi)=1$ and let
$G\in R\setminus\{0\}$ be the Gram determinant of the form with respect to any
$R$-basis of $M$. Then
$$\nu_\pi(G)=\sum_{i>0}\dim_FM_F(i),$$
where $M_F(i)$ are the Jantzen layers of
[[def-jantzen-filtration-of-a-lifted-cell-module]]; in particular the sum is
finite and independent of the chosen basis.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Description of the Jantzen layers: write $x=\sum_ia_ie_i$ in the basis of [F2]. Since $f_1,\dots,f_d$ is an $R$-basis of $M$, the condition $\langle x,yangle\in\pi^kR$ for all $y\in M$ is equivalent to $\langle x,f_jangle\in\pi^kR$ for all $j$; as $\langle x,f_jangle=a_jr_j$, this gives $M(k)=\{\sum_ia_ie_i:
u_\pi(a_ir_i)\ge k\ 	ext{for all }i\}$ with the convention $
u_\pi(0)=\infty$. Reducing modulo $\pi M$, whose basis is $\pi e_1,\dots,\pi e_d$, shows that $M_F(k)$ has as an $F$-basis the images of those $e_i$ with $
u_\pi(r_i)\ge k$: if $
u_\pi(r_i)\ge k$ then the image of $e_i$ lies in $M_F(k)$, while if $
u_\pi(r_i)<k$ then every element of $M(k)$ has $e_i$-coefficient divisible by $\pi$. Hence $\dim_FM_F(k)=\#\{i:
u_\pi(r_i)\ge k\}$. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 Summation: since each $r_i$ is nonzero, the sets $\{k>0:
u_\pi(r_i)\ge k\}$ are finite of cardinality $
u_\pi(r_i)$; by step 1.1 and [F1], $$\sum_{k>0}\dim_FM_F(k)=\sum_{k>0}\#\{i:
u_\pi(r_i)\ge k\}=\sum_i
u_\pi(r_i).$$ [step 1.1, F1]

3.1 Conclusion: by [F3] the right-hand side is $
u_\pi(G)$ for any Gram matrix $G$ of the form in any $R$-basis of $M$; the left-hand side is defined purely in terms of $M$ and the form, so the identity holds for every basis and the sum is finite and basis-independent. [step 2.1, F3] ∎

items.title: The Schur functor sends Weyl and simple modules to Specht and Hecke simple modules
items.statement:
Let $k$ be a field, $q\in k^	imes$, $d\ge n$, and let $\mathcal F(X)=Xe$ be the right-module Schur functor of [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]]. Set $e_q=e(k,q)$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]). For each $\lambda\in\Lambda^+(d,n)$ let $W^\lambda$ be the Weyl module with Schur cell form $B_\lambda$ and nonzero simple head $L^\lambda$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Write $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ and $D_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ for the independent Murphy cell module and its cell-form quotient ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal F(W^\lambda)\cong C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ as right $H$-modules, and this isomorphism identifies $B_\lambda|_{W^\lambda e}$ exactly with the Murphy cell form. 2. $\mathcal F(L^\lambda)\cong D_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$, including the zero quotient; it is nonzero exactly when $\lambda$ is $e_q$-restricted. 3. For every $e_q$-restricted $
u\vdash n$, $$[W^\lambda:L^
u]=[C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):D_{\mathrm M}(
u)].$$

In the page's ordinary Dipper–James normalization ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]], [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]), these identities become $$\mathcal F(W^{\lambda'})\cong(S^\lambda)^	heta,\qquad \mathcal F(L^{\lambda'})\cong(D^\lambda)^	heta.$$ The latter module is nonzero exactly for $e_q$-regular $\lambda$ and is zero otherwise. For $e_q$-regular $
u$, $$[W^{\lambda'}:L^{
u'}]=[S^\lambda:D^
u].$$ The accepted ordinary polytabloid comparison identifies $S^\lambda$ with the historical DJ module $P(\lambda)$ and identifies their form radicals through an explicit unit factor. Thus the dictionary concerns the actual ordinary modules, not merely a renamed cell module. A zero Hecke cell-form quotient is not asserted to be its actual module head. No semisimplicity or choice principle is assumed, and $n=0$ is included.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Under [F1], $\rho(h)\rho(k)=\rho(hk)$ because both act on $H$ by left multiplication, so the identification uses $H$, without an opposite algebra. The functor $X\mapsto Xe$ is exact: for a short exact sequence, a lift $x$ of an element $y\in X''e$ yields the lift $xe$, and an element in the kernel lies in $X'$ and is fixed by $e$, hence lies in $X'e$. The tensor description uses the $(S,eSe)$-bimodule $Se$, which is a direct summand as a left $S$-module. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The support in [F2] gives $e\varphi_{ST}e=\delta_{\operatorname{type}(S),\omega}\delta_{\operatorname{type}(T),\omega}\varphi_{ST}$ and $w_Te=\delta_{\operatorname{type}(T),\omega}w_T$. Semistandard tableaux of type $\omega$ have each label once and are exactly standard tableaux. For standard $s,t$, their defining sum $m_{st}$ has one term, so $\varphi_{st}|_H(a)=m_{st}a$ and $\rho^{-1}(\varphi_{st})=m_{st}$. Thus the higher Schur ideal cuts out exactly $I^{\rhd\lambda}$ in the corner. Read the Schur right-cell law with first index any standard tableau of type $\omega$; coefficient independence permits this choice. Restricting the multiplication by $\rho(h)$ to $H$ gives $m_{st}h$, so its coefficients are the Murphy right-cell coefficients. Consequently $\Psi_\lambda:W^\lambda e\to C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$, $w_t\mapsto c_t$, is an $H$-isomorphism. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 By the Schur cell product, $\varphi_{as}\varphi_{tb}\equiv B_\lambda(w_s,w_t)\varphi_{ab}$ modulo higher Schur shapes, with coefficient independent of the outer indices. Choose all four indices standard of shape $\lambda$ and type $\omega$. They lie in $eSe$; applying $\rho^{-1}$, or evaluating their endomorphisms at $1\in H$, gives $m_{as}m_{tb}\equiv B_\lambda(w_s,w_t)m_{ab}$ modulo $I^{\rhd\lambda}$. The unique coefficient in [F3] is $G_\lambda(c_s,c_t)$, proving $B_\lambda|_{W^\lambda e}=\Psi_\lambda^*G_\lambda$ exactly, with factor $1$. [F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Since $e^*=e$, contravariance gives $B_\lambda(xe,y(1-e))=B_\lambda(x,y(1-e)e)=0$. The decomposition $W^\lambda=W^\lambda e\oplus W^\lambda(1-e)$ is therefore orthogonal. A vector in $W^\lambda e$ pairs trivially with its complement, so it is in the restricted form radical exactly when it lies in $\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}W^\lambda$. Since the latter is an $S$-submodule, $\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}(W^\lambda e)=(\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}W^\lambda)e$. This holds even if the corner form is identically zero. [F2, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 For the canonical semistandard tableau $T^\lambda$ of shape and type $\lambda$, the map $\varphi_{T^\lambda,T^\lambda}$ is the actual projection onto $M^\lambda$: it sends $m_\lambda h$ to itself and is zero on every other summand. Its square equals itself, so the Schur cell product gives $B_\lambda(w_{T^\lambda},w_{T^\lambda})=1$. Hence the Weyl form quotient is nonzero and is its simple head $L^\lambda$ by [F4]. Exactness, step 4.1 and step 3.1 give $L^\lambda e\cong W^\lambda e/(\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}W^\lambda)e\cong C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)/\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)=D_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$, including when this corner quotient is zero. [F2, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 By [F6] and step 5.1, $L^\lambda e\ne0$ precisely for $e_q$-restricted $\lambda$. Apply the exact functor to a finite composition series of $W^\lambda$: every factor $L^\nu$ gives $D_{\mathrm M}(\nu)$ or zero. Delete repeated terms. The remaining factors are the distinct nonzero Murphy simples in [F4], giving $[W^\lambda:L^\nu]=[C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):D_{\mathrm M}(\nu)]$ for each $e_q$-restricted $\nu$. No multiplicity preservation is asserted for a killed simple label. [F4, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Apply [F5] and the involution $\theta$ to obtain $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')\cong(S^\lambda)^\theta$ and $D_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')\cong(D^\lambda)^\theta$. Replacing the Weyl label by $\lambda'$ in steps 2.1 and 5.1 gives the ordinary dictionary, including zero quotients. Conjugation makes $\lambda'$ restricted precisely when $\lambda$ is regular. Twisting both modules by the same exact equivalence preserves composition multiplicities, so step 6.1 gives $[W^{\lambda'}:L^{\nu'}]=[S^\lambda:D^\nu]$ for regular $\nu$. The genuine unit-scaled ordinary form bridge in [F5] also identifies these with the historical DJ polytabloid modules and quotients. At $n=0$, $e=1$ and each form has value $1$, so the same proof includes the empty partition. [F4, F5, F6, step 2.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Separated Hecke residues give seminormal idempotents and bases
items.statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, let $e=e(F,q)$ and assume $e>n$ (with $e=\infty$ allowed); let $\lambda\vdash n$, $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$, and let $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ be the Murphy cell module with Murphy basis $(m_t)_{t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}$ ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]).

1. (**Separation**) If $s,t$ are standard $\lambda$-tableaux with $[\operatorname{content}_s(k)]_q=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q$ for all $1\le k\le n$ then $s=t$. More precisely, if the q-content values agree for all $k\notin\{i,i+1\}$ for some $i$, then $s=t$ or $t=s(i\ i+1)$. 2. (**Idempotents**) Let $\mathcal R_k$ be the set of distinct q-content values of the entry $k$ over standard tableaux of **all** partitions of $n$. For a standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ define $$F_t:=\prod_{k=1}^{n}\ \prod_{\substack{c\in\mathcal R_k\\        c\ne[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q}}        \frac{L_k-c}{[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q-c}\in F[L_1,\ldots,L_n].$$ These are orthogonal idempotents of $H$; their actions on $S_{\mathrm M}^\lambda$ project onto the corresponding simultaneous eigenlines. Put $f_t=m_tF_t$. Then $f_tL_k=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_qf_t$ and $f_t=m_t+\sum_{s\rhd t}a_sm_s$. The global content sets are essential for the asserted idempotency in $H$, rather than only the induced same-shape endomorphisms. 3. (**Orthogonal seminormal basis**) $\{f_t:t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is a basis of $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ satisfying $f_tF_s=\delta_{ts}f_t$ and $\langle f_s,f_t\rangle_\lambda=\delta_{st}\langle f_t,f_t\rangle_\lambda$; it is the **seminormal basis** of the Murphy cell module. 4. (**Generator action**) Let $s$ be a standard $\lambda$-tableau, $1\le i<n$ and $t:=s(i\ i+1)$, and put $\rho:=\operatorname{content}_s(i)-\operatorname{content}_s(i+1)\in\mathbb Z$. If $i$ and $i+1$ lie in the same row of $s$ then $f_sT_i=q\,f_s$; if they lie in the same column then $f_sT_i=-f_s$; otherwise $t$ is standard and $$f_sT_i=\alpha_i(s)\,f_t-\frac{1}{[\rho]_q}f_s,\qquad \alpha_i(s):=\begin{cases}1,&s\rhd t,\\[1mm]\dfrac{[1+\rho]_q[1-\rho]_q}{[\rho]_q[-\rho]_q},&t\rhd s,\end{cases}$$ where $[-\rho]_q$ is the extended quantum integer of [[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]] and for the swapped tableau $\operatorname{content}_t(i)-\operatorname{content}_t(i+1)=-\rho$. No semisimplicity of $H$ is assumed and no choice principle is used.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Reconstruct a tableau from its residue tuple. At a prefix of size $k-1$, two different addable corners have integer content difference of absolute value at most $k$. Since $[a]_q-[b]_q=q^b[a-b]_q$ and $e>n$, their q-contents differ. Starting with the empty diagram, the tuple thus recovers each added node and the final shape. For two tableaux of a fixed shape with identical entries' residues outside $i,i+1$, first reconstruct the common prefix through $i-1$, and reconstruct the common suffix by successively deleting the unique appropriate removable corner from the fixed final shape. The intervening skew diagram has two boxes; its only possible orders are the original order and its swap. This proves both separation assertions. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 Diagonalize the commuting JM operators on a cell. Their triangular basis gives a filtration with one-dimensional joint characters indexed by standard tableaux. Those characters are distinct by step 1.1. For commuting triangular operators, the simultaneous generalized eigenspaces split along their distinct joint characters: the corresponding maximal ideals of the polynomial algebra are pairwise comaximal. Each joint character occurs once in this cell, so each generalized eigenspace is one-dimensional and hence an actual joint eigenline. This finite Chinese-remainder argument works over any field and needs no choice of a generic scalar or algebraic closure. The Lagrange product of the Statement is $1$ on its target tuple and $0$ on every other tuple. Applied to $m_t$, its triangular diagonal coefficient is $1$, and the other possible terms are strictly more dominant. Thus it gives the asserted $f_t$. [F1, step 1.1]

2.2 Compute the diagonal coefficient using the **correctly ordered** JM relation $$T_iL_i=L_{i+1}T_i-(q-1)L_{i+1}-1.$$ For $k\ne i,i+1$, $T_i$ commutes with $L_k$. Consequently separation restricts $f_sT_i$ to the span of $f_s$ and $f_t$ if the swap is standard, or to $f_s$ alone otherwise. Write its coefficient of $f_s$ as $c_s$. The displayed relation gives $$c_s\bigl([\operatorname{content}_s(i)]_q-              [\operatorname{content}_s(i+1)]_q\bigr)    =-(q-1)[\operatorname{content}_s(i+1)]_q-1.$$ Its denominator is $q^{\operatorname{content}_s(i+1)}[\rho]_q$, while the numerator is $-q^{\operatorname{content}_s(i+1)}$, so $c_s=-1/[\rho]_q$. This does not claim that $T_i$ commutes with $L_i$. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 At this stage step 2.1 establishes the projector identities on each individual cell module. The global identities in $H$ will follow below after proving that the sum of the cell modules is faithful. No finite-$e$ classification is a premise. [step 2.1]

3.2 The transition from $m_t$ to $f_t$ is unitriangular, so these vectors form a basis. For $s\ne t$, choose $k$ at which their q-contents differ. Self-adjointness $L_k^*=L_k$ and associativity give $$([\operatorname{content}_s(k)]_q-    [\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q)\langle f_s,f_t\rangle=0.$$ The scalar is nonzero, proving orthogonality. The Lagrange action also gives $f_tF_s=\delta_{ts}f_t$. [F3, step 1.1, step 2.1]

3.3 If the swap is not standard, the consecutive entries lie adjacently in one row or one column. Then $\rho=-1$ or $\rho=1$, respectively, and step 2.2 gives $c_s=q$ or $c_s=-1$. These are the stated row and column cases; the row action is $q$, not the scalar $1$ at a general parameter. [step 2.2]

4.1 Suppose the swap is standard. In the branch $s\rhd t$, the length-additive Murphy action has leading term $m_sT_i=m_t$; the unitriangular eigenbasis change then gives the off-diagonal coefficient $\alpha_i(s)=1$. Higher-dominance terms cannot alter the coefficient at $t$ in this two-dimensional eigenline span. This is the leading-term argument in Mathas's source theorem on the seminormal basis. In both branches the quadratic relation gives $$\alpha_i(s)\alpha_i(t)=q+(q-1)c_s-c_s^2  =\frac{[1+\rho]_q[1-\rho]_q}{[\rho]_q[-\rho]_q}.$$ The last equality follows directly from $[-\rho]_q=-q^{-\rho}[\rho]_q$ and the quantum-integer addition identities. Thus the opposite branch has exactly the displayed coefficient. This proves the generator formula without accepting the inconsistent branch in the 1998 manuscript. [step 3.2, step 2.2]

5.1 Prove nondegeneracy in the separated range locally. The canonical Murphy basis vector has form value $[\lambda]!_q=\prod_a[\lambda_a]!_q$, because $x_\lambda^2=[\lambda]!_qx_\lambda$; its seminormal image has the same value since the canonical tableau is dominance-maximal. This scalar is nonzero when $e>n$. If $s\rhd t=s(i,i+1)$ is a standard swap, put $a=1/[\rho]_q$. Step 4.1 gives $f_t=f_s(T_i+a)$. Associativity, orthogonality and the quadratic relation give $\langle f_t,f_t\rangle=(q+a)(1-a)\langle f_s,f_s\rangle=q[\rho+1]_q[\rho-1]_q[\rho]_q^{-2}\langle f_s,f_s\rangle$. Indeed expansion of $(T_i+a)^2$ and its $f_s$ coefficient $-a$ gives $q-a(q-1)-a^2=(q+a)(1-a)$. The swapped incomparable boxes have $2\le|\rho|\le n-1$: their row and column separations plus one are at most the size of the diagram. Thus all three quantum integers here are nonzero. Every standard tableau is connected to the canonical one by length-increasing swaps of adjacent incomparable entries: bubble-sort its linear extension of the box-order poset into the canonical row-order extension, then reverse the swaps. Induction gives nonzero diagonal norm at every $f_t$, so each cell form is nonsingular. [F2, F3, step 3.2, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Each cell is now its nonzero simple form quotient, absolutely simple, and all these cells are pairwise distinct and exhaust the simple modules by [[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]]. Thus the split semisimple quotient $H/J(H)$ has dimension $\sum_\lambda |\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|^2$. This equals $\dim H$ because the Murphy cellular basis has exactly one element for each pair of standard tableaux of the same shape ([[thm-murphy-tableau-elements-form-a-cellular-basis]]). Hence $J(H)=0$, $H$ is split semisimple, and the direct sum of all its simple cell modules is faithful. On that faithful module the global Lagrange products of the Statement are the orthogonal projectors from step 2.1, with different shapes having disjoint tuples by step 1.1. Therefore $F_sF_t=\delta_{st}F_t$ holds in $H$ itself, proving the global idempotents. This argument proves only the separated range and does not assert a finite-$e$ nonzero-label criterion when $e\le n$. [step 5.1, step 2.1, step 1.1, algebra]

7.1 Steps 1.1-6.1 prove all four claims. No semisimplicity was imposed as a hypothesis: it was derived locally from nondegenerate cells and their complete finite-cell classification. The calculation concerns the intrinsic Murphy cell and keeps the signed ordinary-module dictionary separate. All products and basis changes are finite, and no choice principle is used. [step 1.1, step 3.2, step 4.1, step 6.1] ∎

items.title: Hecke Specht theory specialises to group Specht theory at q = 1
items.statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $q=1\in F$, and let $H_{F,1}(S_n)$ be the specialization of
the generic type-A Hecke algebra at $v\mapsto1$, so that
$H_{F,1}(S_n)\cong F[S_n]$ with $T_w\mapsto w$
([[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]], step 1.1).
Then the Hecke theory of this page specializes as follows.

1. The Murphy elements $m_\mu=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_w$ specialize to the row
   symmetrizers $\sum_{w\in S_\mu}w$, and the Murphy basis $\{m_{st}\}$ of
   $H_{F,1}(S_n)$ specializes to the Murphy basis of the group algebra
   $F[S_n]$ (the base change $\mathbb Z[S_n]\to F[S_n]$ of the integral Murphy
   basis).
2. For every $\lambda\vdash n$ the specialization of the page's Hecke Specht
   module $S^{\lambda}$ ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) is
   the ordinary Specht module in the Dipper-James convention:
   $S^{\lambda}_{q=1}\cong S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}$ as $F[S_n]$-modules, with
   the standard polytabloid basis ([[thm-standard-polytabloid-basis]]); the
   specialized cell form is the standard bilinear form on $S^{\lambda}$ whose
   radical defines the James quotient $D^{\lambda}$
   ([[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]]).
3. The quantum characteristic of $q=1$ is $e=\operatorname{char}(F)$ when
   $\operatorname{char}(F)>0$, and $e=\infty$ when
   $\operatorname{char}(F)=0$
   ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]); in
   characteristic $p>0$ a partition is $e$-regular exactly when it is
   $p$-regular. Hence $D^{\lambda}_{q=1}\ne0$ exactly for $p$-regular $\lambda$
   ([[thm-specht-radical-quotient-is-nonzero-exactly-for-p-regular-partitions]]),
   and for non-$p$-regular $\lambda$ one has
   $\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}=S^{\lambda}$. Over splitting residue fields this also matches the group-side
   classification and conjugate-sign dictionary of
   [[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]] and
   [[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]];
   the assertion here holds over every field by the cellular classification below.
   In characteristic $0$ the specialization is split semisimple and all Specht
   modules are irreducible.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Murphy basis: base change along $\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to F$, $v\mapsto1$, sends $T_w$ to $w$ and $m_\mu=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_w$ to the row symmetrizer $\sum_{w\in S_\mu}w$; the structure constants of the Murphy basis are polynomials in $q$, so they specialize to structure constants in $F[S_n]$ and the specialized family $\{m_{st}\}$ satisfies the cellular axioms over $F$; it is a basis because base change of the free integral Murphy basis is a basis, by [[thm-murphy-tableau-elements-form-a-cellular-basis]]. This is part 1. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Module and form: by [F1] the specialization of the page's Specht module is the ordinary Dipper-James Specht module with the standard polytabloid basis, and the specialized cell form differs from the standard form by the Laurent factor $q^{\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))-\ell(w_\lambda)}$, which is $1$ at $q=1$; hence the two forms agree over every field and have the same radical, so the specialized quotient is the James quotient $D^{\lambda}$. This is part 2. [step 1.1, F1, F2]

3.1 Labels: by [F3], $e=p$ in positive characteristic, and $e$-regular means $p$-regular. Step 2.1 identifies the specialized module and its form exactly with the ordinary group module and form, so the ordinary criterion in [F4] gives precisely the nonzero $p$-regular quotients and the zero form on all other labels, These are all the simples by the cellular classification [F5] and the exact signed-conjugate equivalence of [F1]. In characteristic zero, $e=\infty>n$, so the local separated-range proof in [F4] makes the Murphy cell forms nonsingular and the algebra split semisimple. The exact signed-conjugate unit form dictionary [F1] gives the same conclusion for all ordinary Specht modules. Thus all claims follow over the original field, without using the held finite-$e$ Hecke classifier. [step 2.1, F1, F3, F4, F5] ∎

items.title: The q-Schur Weyl weight-space Gram determinant is a hook product
items.statement:
Let $R$ be an integral domain, $q\in R^\times$, $d,n\ge1$, and let $W^\lambda$ be the Weyl module of $S(d,n)$ for a partition $\lambda\vdash n$ with at most $d$ parts. For a composition $\mu$ of $n$ of length $d$, let $G^\lambda_\mu$ be the Gram determinant of its $\mu$-weight space in the semistandard basis ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Put $\beta_j=\lambda'_j+n-j$ and $h_{ab}=\lambda_a-b+\lambda'_b-a+1$. Then $$G^\lambda_\mu=q^N\prod_{\substack{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda]\\b<c}}  \left(\frac{[h_{ab}]_q}{[h_{ac}]_q}\right)^{  d_\mu(\beta+h_{ac}\mathbf e_b-h_{ac}\mathbf e_c)},$$ where $N=\sum_{T\in T_0(\lambda,\mu)}\ell(d(\operatorname{last}(T)))$. Here $\operatorname{last}(T)$ is the least-dominant standardization in the fiber of $T$, and $d_\mu$ is the exact alternating semistandard number of [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. **Both beta shifts use the same removed hook length $h_{ac}$.**

The exponent is the sorting sign times $|T_0(\eta,\mu)|$ if that balanced beta sequence has distinct nonnegative entries and recovers $\eta$; it is zero otherwise. Equivalently, remove the rim strip $R_{ac}$ and rewrap its $h_{ac}$ boxes with lowest node in column $b$. The sign is the parity of the heights of the removed strip and the newly added strip, the latter measured in the new diagram $\eta$; it is not generally the sum of two old $\lambda$ hook legs ([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]], [[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]).

Form the product first in the universal field $\mathbb Q(Q)$. It equals a Laurent polynomial in $\mathbb Z[Q,Q^{-1}]$, namely the universal integral Gram determinant divided by its displayed unit $Q^N$. Over $R$ the formula means the specialization of that Laurent polynomial. It does not require inverting a vanishing hook number or evaluating $0/0$. All weights and $d<n$ are retained; an empty weight space has determinant $1$.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Preserve small alphabets. Enlarge to $D=\max(d,n)$ temporarily. The sum of permutation summands with types supported on the first $d$ letters is a literal summand of the $D$-alphabet permutation module, with projection $p$ and $pS(D,n)p=S(d,n)$. The normalized maps whose two types have that support, their cell multiplication and their Weyl form coefficients are unchanged. Every semistandard shape with these types has at most $d$ rows. Thus proving the weight norm in the enlarged algebra, where the regular corner exists, proves the original norm as well. No hypothesis $d\ge n$ is added. [given, F1]

1.2 Compute the standard norms. For the canonical standard tableau, $\gamma_{t^\lambda}$ telescopes rowwise to $[\lambda]!_Q$, also its norm by $x_\lambda^2=[\lambda]!_Qx_\lambda$. If $s$ dominates $t=s(i,i+1)$, the adjacent action gives $f_t=f_s(T_i+\alpha)$ with $\alpha=1/[\rho]_Q$. Contravariance, orthogonality and the quadratic relation imply $\langle f_t,f_t\rangle=(Q+\alpha)(1-\alpha) \langle f_s,f_s\rangle$. The two swapped predecessor ratios give $\gamma_t=Q^{-1}(Q+\alpha)(1-\alpha)\gamma_s$: use $[\rho+1]=1+Q[\rho]$ and $[\rho-1]=Q^{-1}([\rho]-1)$. Increasing-length adjacent swaps of incomparable boxes reach every standard tableau, so $\langle f_t,f_t\rangle=Q^{\ell(d(t))}\gamma_t$. [F1, F2]

2.1 Define the cross-weight maps. In the enlarged algebra of step 1.1 let $\omega=(1^n,0^{D-n})$, so $M^\omega=H$. Let $a_\mu:M^\mu\to H$ be inclusion, $a_\mu(m_\mu h)=m_\mu h$, and let $b_\mu:H\to M^\mu$ be $b_\mu(h)=m_\mu h$; both are zero on the other permutation summands. These are actual $H$-linear maps, not maps depending on an unspecified $T$. Under the Hom/intersection coordinate identification of the q-Schur construction, both maps have image coordinate $m_\mu$. Since $m_\mu^*=m_\mu$, the index-swapping star in [F1] gives $a_\mu^*=b_\mu$; this works for compositions as well as partitions. For a standard $s$, composition of its Weyl map with $a_\mu$ evaluates at $m_\mu$ as $m_s m_\mu$, whereas composition of a type-$\mu$ Weyl map with $b_\mu$ evaluates at $1$ as $m_T$. We use right-action composition throughout. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Establish the support and the initial scalar. Write $m_s=m_\lambda T_{d(s)}$ in the Murphy cell. For $s=\operatorname{first}(T)$, $d(s)$ is the least-length double-coset representative for the row blocks of $\lambda$ and $\mu$. The intersection subgroup has one symmetric-group factor of size $c_{iv}=|\{(i,j):T(i,j)=v\}|$ for every nonempty row/label intersection. Decomposing both row subgroups into their distinguished intersection cosets, every reduced coset word occurs once; the remaining intersection sum acts on $m_\lambda$ by its row character $Q^{\ell(w)}$. Hence the exact identity is $$m_s m_\mu=\Bigl(\prod_{i,v}[c_{iv}]!_Q\Bigr)m_T.$$ No factorial is divided out. The same-entry predecessor ratios for this first refinement are $[2]/[1],[3]/[2],\ldots,[c_{iv}]/[c_{iv}-1]$ within each intersection row, so their product $\pi_s$ is exactly that factorial. We also need support after multiplication by $m_\mu$. Filter standard Murphy vectors by the shapes of their prefixes at the ends of the $\mu$ label blocks. Every generator $T_i$ inside such a block preserves this filtration: its row case is multiplication by $Q$; its standard-swap terms have the same block-end prefixes; in its column case the Garnir correction terms have larger tableau-prefix dominance. The last assertion follows by isolating the distinguished term in the length-additive row-coset Garnir identity; all other same-shape terms increase prefix dominance, as proved in [[lem-type-a-hecke-permutation-modules-have-semistandard-murphy-bases-and-specht-filtrations]]. Iterating over each word in $m_\mu$ shows that $m_v m_\mu$ has only coarsened types dominating $\mu(v)$. Its expansion has constant coefficients on semistandard fibers and zero coefficients elsewhere, by the right-hand (starred) permutation-module basis in that supplier. Thus only semistandard $U\unrhd\mu(v)$ occur, strictly if $\mu(v)$ is not semistandard. In particular, if $v\triangleright\operatorname{first}(T)$, every surviving $U$ is strictly above $T$: equality would put $v$ in the fiber of $T$, whose most dominant member is $\operatorname{first}(T)$. This proves the needed support assertion including non-semistandard types. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Determine the scalar on every standardization. Sums of JM elements over a label block commute with that block's row symmetrizer: the adjacent JM relation makes $L_i+L_{i+1}$ commute with $T_i$, and every other $L_j$ commutes with it. The dominance-triangular standard JM action and the support filtration of step 3.1 consequently give triangular block-sum operators on the semistandard maps, with diagonal entries $\sum_{T(i,j)=v}[j-i]_Q$. Their joint eigenvalues distinguish $T$: the Laurent coefficients and the known prefix sizes recover every initial-label content multiset, whose diagonal counts recover its Young diagram. They are self-adjoint, so finite triangular diagonalization gives orthogonal $\psi_T=\varphi_T+$ strictly more dominant terms. The same block-sum identities show that $f_ta_\mu$ lies in the $T$ joint eigenspace whenever $\mu(t)=T$, hence equals $r_t\psi_T$. At $s=\operatorname{first}(T)$, expand $f_s=m_s+$ more dominant standard vectors. Step 3.1 gives coefficient $\pi_s$ at $\varphi_T$ and only higher types in the remaining terms. Thus $r_s=\pi_s$. Now connect standardizations of $T$ by increasing-length adjacent swaps inside each label block; these are the linear extensions of the repeated-label node posets, and bubble sorting gives such a chain from their most dominant extension. If $t=s(i,i+1)$ is one step, [F2] gives $f_t=f_s(T_i+\alpha)$, $\alpha=1/[\rho]_Q$, while $T_i a_\mu=Q a_\mu$ because $T_i m_\mu=Qm_\mu$. Therefore $r_t=(Q+\alpha)r_s$. The only newly included same-entry predecessor pair has content difference $\rho$, so its ratio is $[\rho+1]_Q/[\rho]_Q=Q+\alpha$, proving $\pi_t=(Q+\alpha)\pi_s$. Induction proves the exact identity $f_ta_\mu=\pi_t\psi_T$ for every standardization. [F1, F2, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Determine the last-standardization coefficient and the norm. For $t=\operatorname{last}(T)$, evaluation at $1$ gives $\varphi_Tb_\mu=m_T=\sum_{\mu(v)=T}m_v$. Every other member of this fiber is more dominant than $t$. Also every refinement of $U\triangleright T$ dominates $t$: compare at label-block ends, then use that $t$ is the least-dominant refinement within its own blocks. Consequently the two unitriangular basis changes give $\psi_Tb_\mu=f_t+$ more dominant standard eigenvectors, with coefficient exactly $1$ at $f_t$. At this last refinement the standard predecessor set partitions into the strict semistandard boundary $\Gamma_T$ and same-entry predecessors, so $\gamma_t=\pi_t\gamma_T$. By adjointness of the explicit maps in step 2.1 and orthogonality, $$\pi_t\langle\psi_T,\psi_T\rangle=\langle f_ta_\mu,\psi_T\rangle=\langle f_t,\psi_Tb_\mu\rangle=Q^{\ell(d(t))}\gamma_t.$$ All factors of $\pi_t$ are nonzero over $K$, so $\langle\psi_T,\psi_T\rangle=Q^{\ell(d(t))}\gamma_T$. The transition determinant is $1$, yielding $G^\lambda_\mu=Q^N g^\lambda_\mu$ with $g^\lambda_\mu=\prod_T\gamma_T$. This calculates the cross-weight scalar rather than inferring it from the standard norm alone. [F1, F2, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 4.1]

6.1 Prove the normalized beta product at the level of formal exponents. For $h\ge1$ put $$A_h(\beta,\mu)=-\sum_{b\ne c,\ \beta_b-h<\beta_c}  d_\mu(\beta-h\mathbf e_b+h\mathbf e_c).$$ A nonzero term requires $0\le\beta_b-h$, so the product is finite. Repeated beta entries cancel by exchanging the equal indices; a negative entry cannot become a valid term because, if it is the receiver, the lowered donor is still smaller. Thus these invalid sequences contribute zero exponents. Delete the largest semistandard label, occurring $z$ times in column feet $C$, to get $\beta-\mathbf1_C,\bar\mu$. The strict predecessor boundary excludes every column also in $C$. Consequently the literal exponent $E_h$ in $g$ obeys $$E_h(\beta,\mu)=\sum_{|C|=z}E_h(\beta-\mathbf1_C,\bar\mu)  +\sum_{|C|=z}\sum_{b\notin C,c\in C}  (\mathbf1_{\beta_b-\beta_c+1=h}-\mathbf1_{\beta_b-\beta_c=h})  d_{\bar\mu}(\beta-\mathbf1_C).$$ The final sum is exactly the axial ratio contributed by each deleted largest-label box. [F2, F3, step 5.1]

7.1 Verify the same recurrence for $A_h$. Apply [F3] to its summands and compare with $\sum_C A_h(\beta-\mathbf1_C,\bar\mu)$. Set $\delta=\beta_b-\beta_c-h$. The original condition is $\delta<0$ and the deleted one $\delta-\mathbf1_C(b)+\mathbf1_C(c)<0$. They differ only when $b\in C,c\notin C,\delta=0$ or $b\notin C,c\in C,\delta=-1$. In the first case, exchanging the two shifted beta entries turns the contribution into $-d_{\bar\mu}(\beta-\mathbf1_{C'})$ with $C'=C-b+c$, giving the negative term of step 6.1. In the second case, the exchanged entries give $+d_{\bar\mu}(\beta-\mathbf1_C)$, giving its positive term. Every other case cancels. At degree $0$ both exponent families vanish: a nonzero shifted empty beta sequence would have to exchange two entries with $h=\beta_b-\beta_c$, excluded by the strict condition. Induction gives $E_h=A_h$ and therefore $$g^\lambda_\mu=  \prod_{h\ge1}\prod_{b\ne c,\ \beta_b-h<\beta_c}  [h]_Q^{-d_\mu(\beta-h\mathbf e_b+h\mathbf e_c)}.$$ This proves the regrouping without copying the inconsistent signs in the printed display. [F3, step 6.1]

8.1 Convert to hooks. A surviving lowered bead $\beta_b-h$ is a nonnegative gap, so the bead-gap correspondence makes $h=h_{ab}$ for a node $(a,b)$. The remaining condition $\beta_c>\beta_b-h_{ab}=n-1-\lambda_a+a$ is equivalent to $c\le\lambda_a$; the paired nodes therefore lie in the same row. For $b<c$ write $h=h_{ab}$ and $k=h_{ac}$. Since $h-k=\beta_b-\beta_c$, the two ordered displaced sequences $\beta-h\mathbf e_b+h\mathbf e_c$ and $\beta-k\mathbf e_c+k\mathbf e_b$ exchange their two changed entries. Their signed numbers are negatives of each other, and their factors are exactly $([h]_Q/[k]_Q)^{d_\mu(\beta+k\mathbf e_b-k\mathbf e_c)}$. This proves the stated balanced hook product. Removing and rewrapping the $k$-strip is precisely this bead transfer; sorting counts its crossings, which are the heights of the removed and **new** strips. Colliding or negative sequences vanish by definition. [given, F3, step 7.1]

9.1 Specialize integrally. The semistandard form matrix has entries in $\mathbb Z[Q,Q^{-1}]$, so its determinant and $Q^{-N}G^\lambda_\mu$ are Laurent polynomials. Steps 5.1 and 7.1 identify the rational products with these same polynomials in $\mathbb Q(Q)$. Base change of the free semistandard basis and its form now proves the identity over the given domain, including singular specializations and weights of dimension zero. No individual vanishing ratio is evaluated. All constructions are finite; no choice principle is used. [given, step 5.1, step 7.1, step 8.1] ∎

items.title: The q-Schaper virtual radical-layer formula
items.statement:
Let $R$ be a principal ideal domain, $\pi$ a prime element, $F=R/\pi R$ the residue field, and let $\hat q\in R^{	imes}$ satisfy $[n]!_{\hat q}
e0$ in $R$; put $q:=\hat q+\pi R\in F^{	imes}$. Let $d\ge1$, let $\lambda$ be a partition of $n$ with at most $d$ parts, and let $W^{\lambda}_F$ be the Weyl module of the q-Schur algebra $S_F(d,n)=S(d,n)\otimes_RF$ with its Jantzen filtration $W^{\lambda}_F(i)$ with respect to $(R,\pi)$ ([[def-jantzen-filtration-of-a-lifted-cell-module]], [[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]).

1. (**Jantzen sum formula**) In the Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional $S_F(d,n)$-modules, $$\sum_{i>0} igl[W^{\lambda}_F(i) igr]=\sum_{\substack{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda]\ b<c}}\Bigl(
u_\pi igl([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q} igr)-
u_\pi igl([h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q} igr)\Bigr)\Bigl[W_F^{( eta_1,\dots, eta_b+h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots, eta_c-h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots, eta_n)}\Bigr],$$ where $ eta= eta(\lambda)$ is the beta sequence of $\lambda$, $h^{\lambda}_{ab}$ are its hook lengths and the symbols are the virtual Weyl symbols of [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. 2. (**q-Schaper, $d\ge n$**) If $d\ge n$ and $\Pi$ denotes the Schur functor of [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]], then applying $\Pi$ to (1) gives the corresponding identity for the Hecke Specht modules in the source's normalisation, that is, for the Murphy cell modules $\Pi(W^{\lambda}_F)=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ of [[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]] (the Dipper-James form is obtained by conjugating partitions and applying the same $	heta$ pullback to every Hecke module), $$\sum_{i>0} igl[S^{\lambda}_F(i) igr]=\sum_{\substack{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda]\ b<c}}\Bigl(
u_\pi igl([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q} igr)-
u_\pi igl([h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q} igr)\Bigr)\Bigl[S_F^{( eta_1,\dots, eta_b+h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots, eta_c-h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots, eta_n)}\Bigr]$$ in the Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional $H_{F,q}(S_n)$-modules, with the virtual Specht symbols of [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. The formula is a positive filtration-sum identity expressed in a signed Weyl/Specht basis. A single nonzero signed Weyl coefficient does not force the corresponding labelled simple factor: the entire right side must first be expanded and cancelled in simple classes. For a Weyl module and an off-head label $
u$, the resulting multiplicity of $L^
u$ is an upper bound for $[W^\lambda:L^
u]$, and is positive exactly when that factor occurs in the radical. This does not give a general closed algorithm for decomposition numbers.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Work on a fixed weight space of the lifted free Weyl module. Every hook quantum integer is nonzero because its index is at most $n$ and $[n]!_{\hat q}\ne0$ in the domain. The balanced Gram formula [F1] gives its determinant, and the unit power of $\hat q$ has valuation zero. The Jantzen Gram-valuation lemma [F2] thus gives the sum of positive filtration-submodule dimensions as $$\sum_{(a,b),(a,c),\ b<c}  (\nu_\pi([h_{ab}]_{\hat q})-\nu_\pi([h_{ac}]_{\hat q}))  d_\mu(\beta+h_{ac}\mathbf e_b-h_{ac}\mathbf e_c).$$ The signed number is exactly the weight dimension of the corresponding balanced virtual Weyl symbol, including zero and cutoff cases. [given, F1, F2, F4]

2.1 Apply step 1.1 to every weight. The Weyl weight-character matrix is unitriangular, so [F3] detects equality of Grothendieck classes and proves part 1. These are classes of the filtration submodules $W_F^\lambda(i)$, not their successive quotients and not simply the radical class. [F3, step 1.1]

3.1 Establish filtration transport before applying the exact functor. On the lifted Weyl module $W$, the identity $e^*=e$ makes $We\perp W(1-e)$. For $x\in We$ and every $i\ge0$, pairing $x$ with all of $W$ is divisible by $\pi^i$ exactly when its pairing with $We$ is. Thus $W(i)e=(We)(i)$. Reducing modulo $\pi$ commutes with the direct summand projection, giving $W_F(i)e=(We)_F(i)$. The actual corner isomorphism and factor-$1$ form identity [F5] identify the latter with the Murphy Specht filtration. Applying the exact functor to the proved Weyl-class identity therefore transports each submodule and every signed term, proving part 2 even when a reduced cell form is identically zero. For the ordinary convention, apply the same $\theta$ to both modules and conjugate the labels; the independently proved Laurent-unit form factor preserves these divisibility filtrations as well. [F5, step 2.1]

4.1 Explain the valid multiplicity information. The Weyl form has nonzero simple head, $W_F(1)=\operatorname{rad}W_F$, and $W_F(i)\subseteq\operatorname{rad}W_F$ for $i>0$. Consequently for $\nu\ne\lambda$ its actual multiplicity in $W_F$ is its radical multiplicity, bounded above by its multiplicity in the whole positive sum. This whole-sum multiplicity is positive if and only if that factor occurs in the radical, since the first submodule is the radical and later ones lie inside it. No such conclusion is drawn from an individual positive or negative Weyl coefficient before cancellation. All claims follow from steps 1.1-3.1 and this submodule inclusion. [F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

items.title: General type-A decomposition numbers remain unsolved
items.statement:
The two preceding constraints on the decomposition matrix of $H_{F,q}(S_n)$ are real but limited, and neither solves the general problem.

(i) Dominance unitriangularity ([[cor-type-a-hecke-decomposition-matrix-is-dominance-unitriangular]]) determines only the diagonal entries $d_{\mu\mu}=1$ and the vanishing region $d_{\lambda\mu}\ne0\Rightarrow\mu\unrhd\lambda$; it gives no value for an off-diagonal entry.

(ii) The q-Schaper/Jantzen sum formula ([[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]]) is an identity for the sum of the positive Jantzen filtration submodules. Its individual signed hook terms are not multiplicity bounds. After the whole virtual sum is expanded in simple classes and all cancellations are performed, its nonnegative simple coefficients bound the corresponding radical composition multiplicities from above; it neither determines a general multiplicity nor produces a positive combinatorial rule.

Special coefficient regimes and low-rank calculations determine additional entries (canonically based, weight-one, and small-$n$ cases), and the classification of irreducible Specht modules for symmetric groups in prime characteristic is known (Fayers, Introduction, printed p. 2 of the cited 2012 paper). That classification is distinct from computing all composition multiplicities. No general closed formula for the decomposition numbers of $S_n$ in a fixed positive characteristic is claimed anywhere on this page. This remark records the boundary; it carries no proof obligation and no choice principle.

items.title: Central Hecke Jucys–Murphy scalars separate q-Schur residue contents
items.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative unital ring, $q\in R^\times$, $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, $M=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Lambda(d,n)}M^\alpha$ and $S=\operatorname{End}_H(M)$. For a symmetric polynomial $f$ over $R$, put $z_f=f(L_1,\ldots,L_n)$ for the additive Hecke Jucys–Murphy elements. Right multiplication $\rho_{z_f}:m\mapsto mz_f$ is a central element of $S$. On the right Weyl cell $W^\lambda$ it acts by

$$a_\lambda(f)=f\bigl([c(A)]_q:A\in[\lambda]\bigr),\qquad c(r,s)=s-r.$$

The identity holds over every $R$ and unit $q$, without division by a quantum integer or a Gram determinant. In particular, if $R=F$ is a field of finite quantum characteristic $e\ge2$ and $L^\mu$ is a constituent of $W^\lambda$, then $\lambda$ and $\mu$ have the same multiset of residues $c(A)\bmod e$. Neither partition is required to be restricted or to survive the Hecke corner. This proves a necessary content-separation condition, not an assertion that equal content is sufficient for common-block membership.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Work first over $A=\mathbb Z[u,u^{-1}]$ with fraction field $K=\mathbb Q(u)$. The regular trace pairing $(a,b)\mapsto\operatorname{Tr}(\ell_{ab})$ has entries in $A$ in the standard Hecke basis. At $u=1$ its matrix is $n!\,\delta_{v,w^{-1}}$, so its determinant is nonzero and it is nondegenerate over $K$. If $a$ belongs to the Jacobson radical, $ab$ is nilpotent for every $b$ by [F4]; its left multiplication is nilpotent and has trace zero. Nondegeneracy forces the radical to vanish. Thus $H_K$ is semisimple. Its shape-$\lambda$ cell layer has the multiplication $XG_\lambda Y$ of [F1]. If $G_\lambda$ were singular, the nonzero subspace $\{X:G_\lambda X=0\}$ would be a two-sided ideal with square zero, contradicting [F4]. Hence $G_\lambda$ is invertible and $X\mapsto G_\lambda X$ identifies this layer with a full matrix algebra over $K$. [F1, F4, algebra]

1.2 Construct an injective right $S$-module map $j:W^\lambda\to\operatorname{Hom}_H(M,C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda))$. Project the output of $\varphi_{T^\lambda T}:M\to M^\lambda$ through $\pi:M^\lambda\to C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)=M^\lambda/(M^\lambda\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$. For $T$ of type $\nu$, the resulting map is zero on the other summands and sends $m_\nu$ to $m_T=\sum_{t:\nu(t)=T}m_t$. Higher Schur maps with output type $\lambda$ have Hecke values of strictly dominant shape, so their output is killed by $\pi$. Thus this assignment respects the cell quotient and multiplication by any $s\in S$ becomes composition on the right: $j(ws)=j(w)\circ s$. For each fixed type the sets of standard $t$ with $\nu(t)=T$ are disjoint. Each is nonempty: standardize equal entries of a semistandard tableau in increasing column order; equal entries cannot share a column, row order is retained, and different entries occupy disjoint consecutive label blocks. Hence their sums $m_T$ are independent in the free Murphy cell basis, over every $R$. This proves injectivity, including zero type entries. No surjectivity onto all specialized Hom spaces is asserted. [F1, F3, algebra, construct]

2.1 For an integral symmetric polynomial $f$, $z_f$ is central by [F2]. Its action on the generic cell layer is a bimodule endomorphism of that full matrix algebra, hence scalar: its value at the identity commutes with every matrix and the rest follows by multiplication. Accordingly its matrix on $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)_K$ is scalar. The triangular matrices in [F2] give its diagonal as $f([c_t(1)]_u,\ldots,[c_t(n)]_u)$, equal to $a_\lambda(f)$ for every $t$ because $f$ is symmetric and the node multiset is fixed. Thus $z_f$ acts exactly by this scalar. Both sides have matrices over $A$, and injection into $K$ proves the identity before specialization. Every symmetric polynomial over an arbitrary $R$ is an $R$-linear combination of integral monomial symmetric polynomials: coefficients are constant on each monomial orbit. Apply the integral identities to these monomial polynomials and specialize $u\mapsto q$. Therefore every $z_f$ acts by $a_\lambda(f)$ on the actual Murphy cell over $R$, including singular parameters. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For central $z_f\in H$, right multiplication preserves every $M^\alpha$ and is $H$-linear. Every $H$-linear endomorphism $s$ of $M$ satisfies $s(mz_f)=s(m)z_f$, so $\rho_{z_f}$ is central in $S$. For $w\in W^\lambda$ and $m\in M$, step 1.2 and $H$-linearity give $$j(w\rho_{z_f})(m)=j(w)(mz_f)=j(w)(m)z_f=a_\lambda(f)j(w)(m),$$ the last equality by step 2.1. Injectivity gives $w\rho_{z_f}=a_\lambda(f)w$, proving the full ring-level assertion. If $M=0$ all cell assertions are empty. At rank zero the empty cell is $R$ with the empty polynomial evaluation, so the same conclusion holds. [F2, F3, step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra]

4.1 Suppose now that $R=F$ and $L^\mu$ is a constituent of $W^\lambda$. Step 3.1 gives scalar $a_\lambda(f)$ on this constituent. Since $L^\mu$ is the nonzero quotient of $W^\mu$ by [F3], its scalar is also $a_\mu(f)$; hence they agree for every symmetric $f$. Taking all elementary symmetric polynomials gives $$\prod_{A\in[\lambda]}(X-[c(A)]_q)=\prod_{B\in[\mu]}(X-[c(B)]_q).$$ By [F5], if $q=1$ the distinct $e$ residues are the distinct prime-field values $[c]_1$; if $q\ne1$, $[a]_q=[b]_q$ is equivalent to $q^a=q^b$, hence to $a\equiv b\pmod e$. Unique factorization of these monic products into distinct field-linear factors therefore gives equality of every residue multiplicity, also when the field characteristic divides a multiplicity. There is no restriction on either label's Hecke-corner image, and no splitting extension, Gram division or choice principle enters the argument. [F3, F5, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Residue sequences need not separate when e is at most n
items.statement: The hypothesis $e>n$ in [[thm-separated-hecke-residues-give-seminormal-idempotents-and-bases]] cannot be dropped. Take $F=\mathbb C$, $q=-1$ (so $e=e(\mathbb C,-1)=2$, [[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]), $n=3$ and $\lambda=(2,1)$. The two distinct standard tableaux $s=\begin{smallmatrix}1&2\\3\end{smallmatrix}$ and $t=\begin{smallmatrix}1&3\\2\end{smallmatrix}$ have contents $\operatorname{content}_s(1),\operatorname{content}_s(2),\operatorname{content}_s(3)=0,1,-1$ and $\operatorname{content}_t(1),\operatorname{content}_t(2),\operatorname{content}_t(3)=0,-1,1$, and the extended quantum-integer identity gives $[1]_{-1}=1=[-1]_{-1}$, since $[-1]_{-1}=-(-1)^{-1}[1]_{-1}=1$. Hence $$([\operatorname{content}_s(k)]_q)_{k=1,2,3}=(0,1,1)=([\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q)_{k=1,2,3}\quad(q=-1):$$ the q-content sequences collide although $s\ne t$, so the separation conclusion of the theorem fails. The difference of the two putative separating eigenvalues at $k=2$ is $[-1]_{-1}-[1]_{-1}=0$. Thus interpolation cannot distinguish the two tableaux: a formula that excludes equal values may still define a polynomial, but it is not a separating projector for these two labels. The attempted generator formula has axial distance $\rho=2$ and $[\rho]_{-1}=0$. In fact $L_2$ has a nontrivial Jordan block on this cell, so this cell has no simultaneous JM-eigenbasis. This explicit example shows that the uniform separation hypothesis $e>n$ cannot be dropped; it does not claim that every individual cell at every parameter with $e\le n$ lacks a seminormal basis. At the boundary $e=n=2$, still over $\mathbb C$ with $q=-1$, the row and column tableaux both have tuple $(0,1)$. The global Lagrange products in the theorem are consequently $1$ for both labels, so they are not orthogonal. Thus even the proposed replacement $e\ge n$ fails for the full global-idempotent statement.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The field $\mathbb C$, $q=-1\in\mathbb C^{\times}$, the primary case $n=3$ and the boundary test $n=2$, the standard tableaux $s,t$ of shape $(2,1)$ above, and the q-integers of [[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]].

[F1] ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]) $e(\mathbb C,-1)=2$: the least $m\ge1$ with $[m]_{-1}=0$ is $m=2$, since $[2]_{-1}=1+q=0$ and $[1]_{-1}=1\ne0$.

[F2] ([[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]]) The q-content value of an entry is $[\operatorname{content}]_q$ with $[m]_q=1+q+\cdots+q^{m-1}$ for $m\ge0$ and $[-m]_q=-q^{-m}[m]_q$ for $m>0$; at $q=-1$ one has $[1]_{-1}=1$ and $[-1]_{-1}=-(-1)^{-1}[1]_{-1}=1$.

[F3] ([[thm-separated-hecke-residues-give-seminormal-idempotents-and-bases]]) Under the hypothesis $e>n$ the q-content sequence determines the standard tableau, and the denominators of the spectral projectors are nonzero.




## Counterexample

1.1 Contents of the two tableaux: for $s$ with rows $(1,2)$ and $(3)$ the nodes are $(1,1),(1,2),(2,1)$ for $1,2,3$, giving contents $0,1,-1$; for $t$ with rows $(1,3)$ and $(2)$ the nodes are $(1,1),(2,1),(1,2)$ for $1,2,3$, giving contents $0,-1,1$. [given]

2.1 Collision: by [F1] and [F2], $[2]_{-1}=0$ and $[1]_{-1}=[-1]_{-1}=1$; hence $[\operatorname{content}_s(1)]_{q}=0=[\operatorname{content}_t(1)]_q$, $[\operatorname{content}_s(2)]_q=1=[\operatorname{content}_t(2)]_q$ and $[\operatorname{content}_s(3)]_q=1=[\operatorname{content}_t(3)]_q$, so the two q-content sequences coincide even though $s\ne t$. [step 1.1, F1, F2]

3.1 Interpolation and axial distance. The eigenvalue difference that would be needed to distinguish $s$ and $t$ at $k=2$ is $1-1=0$. Equal-value exclusion in a polynomial product does not make its literal denominators zero; it instead loses the factor that could distinguish these tuples. No polynomial in the JM operators can provide the two distinct joint-eigenvalue labels used in the separated-range construction. For the swap of $2$ and $3$, $\rho=1-(-1)=2$ and $[2]_{-1}=0$, so the displayed separated-range generator formula is undefined here. [step 2.1, F1, F3]

4.1 Verify the failure of a JM-eigenbasis on this cell directly. Put $m_s=1+T_1$ and $m_t=(1+T_1)T_2$ modulo the higher row-shape ideal. The quadratic relation gives $m_sT_1=q m_s$. The higher row symmetrizer is $1+T_1+T_2+T_1T_2+T_2T_1+T_1T_2T_1$, so its vanishing in this cell gives $m_tT_1=-m_s-m_t$. At $q=-1$, since $L_2=q^{-1}T_1=-T_1$, it follows that $m_sL_2=m_s$ and $m_tL_2=m_s+m_t$. Thus $L_2-I$ is nonzero and $(L_2-I)^2=0$ on this two-dimensional cell. It is not diagonalizable over $\mathbb C$, so a simultaneous JM-eigenbasis cannot exist on this cell. Together with step 2.1 this supplies the claimed concrete boundary counterexample, without making a universal claim about all cells outside the separated range. [given, F2, step 2.1, step 3.1]

5.1 Check the boundary case $n=e=2$. The row and column tableaux have contents $(0,1)$ and $(0,-1)$, whose q-content tuples both equal $(0,1)$ at $q=-1$ by [F2]. These are all standard tableaux of size two, so the theorem's global sets are $\mathcal R_1=\{0\}$ and $\mathcal R_2=\{1\}$. For either label every inner product in its Lagrange formula is empty, giving $F_{\rm row}=F_{\rm column}=1$. Their product is $1\ne0$ in the nonzero algebra $H_{\mathbb C,-1}(S_2)$, which has basis $1,T_1$. Hence they are not orthogonal, disproving replacement of $e>n$ by $e\ge n$ in the global theorem. This supplements the same-shape collision and Jordan block at size three. [given, F2, F3, step 2.1] ∎

items.title: The Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements through rank four
items.statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $q\in R^{\times}$. In $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ the Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements ([[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]]) for $n\ge4$ are $$L_1=0,\quad L_2=q^{-1}T_{(1,2)},\quad L_3=q^{-1}T_{(2,3)}+q^{-2}T_{(1,3)},\quad L_4=q^{-1}T_{(3,4)}+q^{-2}T_{(2,4)}+q^{-3}T_{(1,4)},$$ and in general $L_k=\sum_{j<k}q^{j-k}T_{(j,k)}$. For the standard tableau $t=\begin{smallmatrix}1&3&4\\2\end{smallmatrix}$ of shape $(3,1)$ the contents of the entries $k=1,2,3,4$ are $0,-1,1,2$ ([[def-content-vector-of-a-standard-tableau]]), so the diagonal eigenvalues of $L_1,\dots,L_4$ on the Murphy vector $m_t$ are $[0]_q=0$, $[-1]_q=-q^{-1}$, $[1]_q=1$ and $[2]_q=1+q$; the triangular correction terms $\sum_{v\rhd t}a_vm_v$ are present in general ([[thm-hecke-jucys-murphy-action-is-dominance-triangular]]) in the Murphy basis, even in the semisimple range. In the separated range, replacing $m_t$ by the seminormal vector $f_t$ removes these correction terms, as proved in [[thm-separated-hecke-residues-give-seminormal-idempotents-and-bases]]. At $q=1$ the four elements specialize to the ordinary Jucys-Murphy elements $X_1=0$, $X_2=(1\,2)$, $X_3=(1\,3)+(2\,3)$, $X_4=(1\,4)+(2\,4)+(3\,4)$ and the eigenvalues to $0,-1,1,2$, the standard contents of $t$.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A commutative ring $R$, $q\in R^{\times}$, the Hecke algebra $H_{R,q}(S_n)$, the Jucys-Murphy elements and q-contents ([[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]]), the content vector of a standard tableau ([[def-content-vector-of-a-standard-tableau]]), and the q=1 specialization $H_{R,1}(S_n)\cong R[S_n]$ ([[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]]).

[F1] ([[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]]) $L_k=\sum_{j<k}q^{j-k}T_{(j,k)}$; $[m]_q=1+q+\cdots+q^{m-1}$ for $m\ge0$, $[-m]_q=-q^{-m}[m]_q$ for $m>0$, and $[m]_1=m$ for all $m\in\mathbb Z$.

[F2] ([[thm-hecke-jucys-murphy-action-is-dominance-triangular]]) $m_tL_k=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q\,m_t+\sum_{v\rhd t}a_vm_v$ on the Murphy cell module, so the displayed values are the diagonal entries and the correction terms are as stated.



## Verification

1.1 Substitution: in [F1], for $k=1$ the sum is empty, giving $L_1=0$; for $k=2$ it has the single term $q^{1-2}T_{(1,2)}=q^{-1}T_{(1,2)}$; for $k=3$ it has $q^{-1}T_{(2,3)}+q^{-2}T_{(1,3)}$; and for $k=4$ it has $q^{-1}T_{(3,4)}+q^{-2}T_{(2,4)}+q^{-3}T_{(1,4)}$, matching the displayed list. [given, F1]

1.2 Contents: reading the tableau $t$ with rows $(1,3,4)$ and $(2)$, the node of $1$ is $(1,1)$ with content $1-1=0$, the node of $2$ is $(2,1)$ with content $1-2=-1$, the node of $3$ is $(1,2)$ with content $2-1=1$ and the node of $4$ is $(1,3)$ with content $3-1=2$; by definition $[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q$ is the q-integer of these contents. [given, F1]

2.1 Eigenvalues: by [F1], $[0]_q=0$, $[-1]_q=-q^{-1}[1]_q=-q^{-1}$, $[1]_q=1$ and $[2]_q=1+q$; substituting into the triangularity formula [F2] gives the stated diagonal eigenvalues $0,-1,1,2$ up to the q-powers $-q^{-1},1,1+q$. The correction terms are exactly the sum $\sum_{v\rhd t}a_vm_v$ of [F2] and are not asserted to vanish outside the semisimple range. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F1, F2]

3.1 Specialization: setting $q=1$ in the displayed formulas turns $L_k$ into $\sum_{j<k}(j\,k)=X_k$ by the specialization isomorphism of [[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]] and [F1], giving $X_1=0$, $X_2=(1\,2)$, $X_3=(1\,3)+(2\,3)$ and $X_4=(1\,4)+(2\,4)+(3\,4)$; the eigenvalues $[m]_1=m$ become $0,-1,1,2$, the contents of $t$. [step 1.2, step 2.1, F1] ∎

items.title: The Murphy cellular basis of H(S_3)
items.statement:
Work over any commutative ring $R$ with $q\in R^{\times}$ and let $H=H_{R,q}(S_3)$
with generators $T_1,T_2$, the braid relation $T_1T_2T_1=T_2T_1T_2$ and
quadratics $T_i^2=(q-1)T_i+q$. The Murphy cellular basis
([[thm-murphy-tableau-elements-form-a-cellular-basis]]) is indexed by the
partitions $(3),(2,1),(1^3)$ ordered by dominance. Explicitly, with $*$ the
antiautomorphism $T_w^*=T_{w^{-1}}$
([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]): (a) for $\lambda=(3)$,
$\mathrm{Std}(3)=\{s\}$ and
$m_{ss}=m_{(3)}=1+T_1+T_2+T_1T_2+T_2T_1+T_1T_2T_1$; (b) for $\lambda=(2,1)$,
$\mathrm{Std}(2,1)=\{t,u\}$ with $t=\begin{smallmatrix}1&2\\3\end{smallmatrix}$,
$u=\begin{smallmatrix}1&3\\2\end{smallmatrix}$, and $m_{(2,1)}=1+T_1$ (the row
symmetrizer of $S_{(2,1)}=\langle(1\,2)\rangle$), so that $m_{tt}=1+T_1$,
$m_{tu}=(1+T_1)T_2$, $m_{ut}=T_2(1+T_1)$ and $m_{uu}=T_2(1+T_1)T_2$; (c) for
$\lambda=(1^3)$, $\mathrm{Std}(1^3)=\{v\}$ and $m_{vv}=m_{(1^3)}=1$. In total
$1+4+1=6=3!=|S_3|$ elements; the middle cell carries
$|\mathrm{Std}(2,1)|^2=4$ basis elements, its two off-diagonal elements
satisfy $m_{tu}^*=m_{ut}$, and the largest cell is spanned by $m_{ss}$,
illustrating the cellular anti-involution. At $q=1$ this is the Murphy basis of
$R[S_3]$, obtained by base change from the integral basis over $\mathbb Z$
([[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]]).
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A commutative ring $R$, $q\in R^{\times}$, $H=H_{R,q}(S_3)$ with standard basis $\{T_w\}$ and Murphy elements ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]); the cellular axioms ([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]); the Murphy cellular basis theorem ([[thm-murphy-tableau-elements-form-a-cellular-basis]]).

[F1] ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]) $m_\mu=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_w$, $m_{st}=T_{d(s)}^*m_\mu T_{d(t)}$, $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$; for the shape $(2,1)$ the distinguished representatives are $d(t)=1$ and $d(u)=s_2$, and for $(3)$ and $(1^3)$ the Young subgroups are all of $S_3$ and trivial respectively.

[F2] ([[thm-murphy-tableau-elements-form-a-cellular-basis]]) The six elements $m_{st}$ form an $R$-basis of $H$ indexed by the three partitions ordered by dominance.

[F3] At $q=1$, $T_w\mapsto w$ identifies $H_{R,1}(S_3)$ with $R[S_3]$ over every commutative $R$ ([[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]], Definition, final paragraph). The integral Murphy basis specializes by [F2].



## Verification

1.1 Cell $(2,1)$: $S_{(2,1)}=\langle s_1\rangle$, so $m_{(2,1)}=1+T_1$; the two standard tableaux of shape $(2,1)$ are $t=\begin{smallmatrix}1&2\\3\end{smallmatrix}$ (row reading word $1\,2\,3$, so $d(t)=1$) and $u=\begin{smallmatrix}1&3\\2\end{smallmatrix}$ (row reading word $1\,3\,2$, so $d(u)=s_2$). Hence $m_{tt}=1\cdot(1+T_1)\cdot1=1+T_1$, $m_{tu}=(1+T_1)T_2$, $m_{ut}=T_2^*(1+T_1)=T_2(1+T_1)$ and $m_{uu}=T_2^*(1+T_1)T_2=T_2(1+T_1)T_2$, using $T_2^*=T_2$ and $m_{(2,1)}^*=m_{(2,1)}$. [given, F1]

1.2 Cells $(3)$ and $(1^3)$: $S_{(3)}=S_3$ has six elements with reduced expressions $1,s_1,s_2,s_1s_2,s_2s_1,s_1s_2s_1$, so $m_{(3)}=1+T_1+T_2+T_1T_2+T_2T_1+T_1T_2T_1=T_{d(s)}^*m_{(3)}T_{d(s)}$ for the unique standard tableau; $S_{(1^3)}$ is trivial, so its group algebra sum is the identity, $m_{(1^3)}=1$, and $m_{vv}=1$. [given, F1]

2.1 Count and anti-involution: the three cells contribute $1^2+2^2+1^2=6=3!=|S_3|$ elements, in agreement with $H$ being free of rank $6$; and $m_{tu}^*=m_{ut}$ is the instance of the general identity $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$ of [F1], the middle cell being the one with two indices. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F1, F2]

3.1 Specialization: setting $q=1$ turns $T_w$ into $w$, so the displayed elements become the Murphy basis of $R[S_3]$; this is the $n=3$ case of [F3]. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F3] ∎

items.title: The q-Schaper calculation for (3,2) at e = 2
items.statement:
Take $R=\mathbb C[\hat q]_{(1+\hat q)}$, the prime element $\pi=1+\hat q$ (so that $F=\mathbb C$ and $q:=\hat q+\pi R$ specialises to $-1$, giving $e=2$), and $\lambda=(3,2)$, $n=5$. Evaluating the q-Schaper virtual sums ([[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]], [[thm-q-schur-weyl-weight-space-gram-determinant-hook-product]], [[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]], [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]], [[lem-dj-bridge-integral-murphy-and-polytabloid-straightening]], [[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]]) with the hook valuations $
u_\pi([2]_{\hat q})=
u_\pi([4]_{\hat q})=1$, $
u_\pi([3]_{\hat q})=
